lead.headline: Ukraine and Russia emergency alert apps hacked as local truce ends
lead.dek: False nuclear, chemical and missile warnings reached phones on both sides of the front within hours of each other.
body: Emergency alert apps in both Ukraine and Russia were hit by cyberattacks at the turn of the weekend, pushing false warnings to ordinary users, according to officials from both countries and reports from Reuters, the Associated Press and Al Jazeera.

In Ukraine, the national air raid alert app showed fake notices late on Sunday, 1 November, claiming nuclear and chemical threats around Kyiv and warning of street fighting. One message said Russia had deployed its Oreshnik hypersonic missile. The Ukrainian Air Force said the app appeared to have been subjected to "enemy influence", told residents there was no radiation threat and urged calm. AP reported that the alerts appeared in English, Russian and Ukrainian, that the English versions contained spelling and grammar mistakes, and that the app was briefly suspended and then restored. Air force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said the incident did not affect security or defence operations, and sirens and other warning channels kept working.

Early on Monday, Russia's Emergencies Ministry said its own mobile app had suffered a large cyberattack that spread false information. AP said a false alert went out at about 2:45 a.m. Moscow time and reached 33 of Russia's 89 regions, while the ministry said it had identified the vulnerability and was taking steps to fix it. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said state bodies face constant cyber threats, including some that use artificial intelligence.

Neither government has said who was behind the attack on Russia's app. Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications blamed Russia for the hack of the Ukrainian app. AP noted that a Russian Telegram channel linked to the security services credited a hacking group called Hitcore with the Ukrainian breach, a claim AP could not verify. Reuters said it was unclear whether the two incidents were connected.

The incidents came as a rare local truce was ending in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region. AP said the pause began on 27 October to allow humanitarian aid and evacuations, and described it as the most significant truce between the two sides since the full-scale invasion began; Al Jazeera reported that it ended on Sunday. Ukraine's general staff said Russia used the lull to reinforce drone defences and restock ammunition. Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, the lead civilian negotiator, had hoped the arrangement could be a model for wider efforts and support three-way talks with Russia and the United States expected this month.

Fighting continued elsewhere. Ukrainian officials said drone strikes injured 12 people in Kharkiv and five in Odesa, while Russia's Defence Ministry said it shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight and the governor of Samara said air defences were repelling an attack. In Kherson, regional authorities said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were taken to hospital with blast injuries as the truce lapsed.
lead.why: Alert systems are meant to be trusted in seconds, so tampering with them is a way to sow fear without firing a shot. The episode also shows how fragile the one durable pause in the war was.

facts.who: Ukraine's air force and Russia's Emergencies Ministry
facts.what: False nuclear, chemical and missile alerts sent through both countries' emergency apps
facts.when: Late on 1 November (Ukraine) and early on 2 November (Russia)
facts.why: Both apps were hacked; who did it has not been established

lead.differ: Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications blamed Russia for the Ukrainian hack, while AP said a Russian Telegram channel credited a group called Hitcore, a claim AP could not verify. AP said the Oleshky truce began on 27 October; Al Jazeera said it ended on Sunday.
lead.watch: Three-way talks with Russia and the United States that Ukraine expected this month, and whether either government names who was behind the hacks.

more.headline: Marvell agrees $115 billion all-stock deal for Lumentum
more.dek: The chipmaker is betting that optical connectivity will define the next phase of AI data centres, and its investors were not impressed.
body: Marvell Technology said on Monday it will buy Lumentum in an all-stock transaction with an implied enterprise value of about $115 billion, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Each Lumentum share will convert into 4.5 Marvell shares, or roughly $1,132 per share at announcement, a premium of about 23.9 percent to the unaffected prices of 28 October.

Marvell holders would own about 67 percent of the combined company and Lumentum holders about 33 percent. Marvell chief executive Matt Murphy would stay on as chairman and chief executive, and three Lumentum directors, including chief executive Michael Hurlston, would join the board. The companies said the deal targets a $550 billion market and more than $1 billion in annual cost savings, and expect it to add to Marvell's adjusted earnings per share in the first year. Closing needs shareholder and regulatory approval and is expected in the first half of 2028.

Markets reacted coolly. The Next Web, citing Reuters, reported Lumentum shares down about 10 percent and Marvell about 5 percent on Monday morning, after Marvell had already fallen sharply since talks were first reported. The site, citing Bloomberg, called it the year's largest deal by equity value.
more.why: The deal signals how much money is flowing into the plumbing of AI infrastructure, and the long closing timeline leaves regulators years to weigh in.

facts.what: An all-stock takeover of Lumentum by Marvell
facts.how: 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share

more.watch: Shareholder and regulatory approvals; the companies expect the deal to close in the first half of 2028.
more.india: If AI data-centre spending keeps growing this fast, companies that build or run data centres in India could feel the effects on equipment costs and supply.

more.headline: Elizabeth Holmes documentary tops a sleepy Halloween box office
more.dek: A24's three-hour film edged a DC superhero release in a weekend that was among the year's weakest.
body: "You Can See Everything", a documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, took first place at the North American box office for the first time in its third weekend, according to studio estimates reported by the Associated Press.

It earned an estimated $10.6 million from 2,655 locations, just ahead of Warner Bros.' DC film "Clayface" at $10.4 million, which fell 57 percent in its second weekend. The documentary has made about $63.9 million domestically on a reported $7 million budget. LAIKA's "Wildwood" was third with $7.5 million.

Total ticket sales were estimated at under $56 million, which AP said would be the second-lowest weekend of the year, as Halloween on Saturday kept people away from theatres. Domestic takings remain more than 17 percent above last year. Final figures were due on Monday; industry sites reported slightly different numbers, so the estimates here may shift.
more.why: A long, low-budget documentary beating a studio franchise film is a rare result, and a reminder that audiences are still choosing selectively.

facts.what: A documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes topped the North American box office
facts.when: The Halloween weekend, 30 October to 1 November

more.differ: Industry sites reported slightly different weekend numbers from the studio estimates reported by AP; final figures were due on Monday.
more.watch: Final weekend figures, and whether the film holds its audience.

lead.headline: Democrats seize House and Senate in midterm rebuke of Trump
lead.dek: Voters ended Republican control of Congress on election night, flipping at least seven Senate seats and the House, according to Al Jazeera and other outlets.
body: Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections held on Tuesday 3 November 2026, ending the Republican trifecta that followed the 2024 election. Al Jazeera reported that the Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats late on Tuesday, and that the House was also called for the party late that night.

The scale became clearer by early Wednesday. Cox Media Group's stations reported Democrats leading 228 to 139 in the House with several races uncalled, after a gain of 19 seats, and on pace for their biggest majority since 2008. In the Senate they stood at 54 to 44 with two contests undecided. Al Jazeera said the outgoing Senate was 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats and two independents who caucus with Democrats, so the party needed a net gain of four seats and had flipped at least seven. Alaska, where Dan Sullivan held a narrow edge over Mary Peltola, and Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom was marginally ahead of Cindy Hyde-Smith, were still being counted at that point.

The flipped Senate seats included several that Republicans had held for decades. Al Jazeera listed James Talarico over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Sherrod Brown over Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Adam Hamilton over Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, Josh Turek over Ashley Hinson in Iowa, Annie Andrews in South Carolina, and Troy Jackson over Sen. Susan Collins in Maine. Democrats also held Georgia through Jon Ossoff and Virginia through Mark Warner, and Abdul El-Sayed beat Mike Rogers in Michigan. In the House, races reported as Democratic gains included Iowa's 3rd District and Pennsylvania's 10th, where Janelle Stelson defeated Rep. Scott Perry.

Reactions split along predictable lines. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become Speaker, said voters had "had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption." Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called it a generational remake of the Senate map, while Speaker Mike Johnson said keeping the House would have defied more than a century of midterm history. Al Jazeera reported that President Donald Trump said Democrats had fought hard and suggested the US-Israel war on Iran and higher petrol prices probably played a part, while also posting that he was not on the ballot.

Trump said he holds total veto power and expects Democrats to send him bills he called insane, which he said he would veto, adding that they would come back to negotiate after a few months. The new Congress is scheduled to be sworn in on 3 January 2027, when Democrats can begin using their majorities to stall legislation and hold up nominations. Final tallies, including the close Alaska and Mississippi Senate races and remaining House seats, were still to be settled in the days after election night.
lead.why: Divided government will reshape what Washington can pass or block for Trump's final two years, and shows how voters judged his economy and Iran policies.

facts.who: US voters, the Democratic and Republican parties
facts.what: Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate
facts.why: Trump said the Iran war and higher petrol prices probably played a part

lead.differ: Seat counts differed between outlets on election night; the House figures used here were a partial count from early Wednesday.
lead.watch: The close Alaska and Mississippi Senate races, and the new Congress being sworn in on 3 January 2027.
lead.india: A divided Washington could slow or change US trade, tariff and visa decisions that matter to Indian businesses and students.

more.headline: Fridge-hacking wave reaches UK meat suppliers
more.dek: Cyberattacks that overheated supermarket refrigeration across Europe also hit a few British firms, officials said.
body: Hackers who raised temperatures in internet-connected fridges and freezers at supermarkets across Europe also reached UK firms, the Press Association reported on 3 November. Al Jazeera said units at more than 100 shops in several countries overheated on Monday 2 November, including Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, seven Coop stores in Sweden and 13 SuperValu stores in Ireland. Hundreds of French supermarkets were hit in October. Nobody has claimed responsibility.

In Britain the Association of Independent Meat Suppliers said a few of its roughly 300 members were affected, but the units were empty and no meat was lost. The Record reported the attackers used Copeland XWEB controllers; Copeland confirmed some products are affected, and a firmware fix has been available since August. The National Cyber Security Centre called the national impact minimal and said it is too early to say who was responsible.

The centre's chief executive, Richard Horne, said the UK had done "tech on the cheap" for decades, and warned other systems such as refrigeration, sluice gates and power switching face similar exposure. EU farm commissioner Christophe Hansen called the attacks a deliberate attempt to disrupt food supply, though he said food security was not at risk.
more.why: The incidents show how unpatched, internet-facing control systems can be turned against everyday infrastructure, with no sophisticated tools needed.

facts.what: Hackers raised temperatures in internet-connected supermarket fridges and freezers
facts.where: Supermarkets across Europe, and a few UK meat suppliers
facts.when: 2 November, with UK impact reported on 3 November

more.watch: Whether anyone claims the attacks, and how fast shops install the firmware fix that has been available since August.

more.headline: Manchester United storm back from two down to beat Roma
more.dek: Matheus Cunha scored twice late on as United won 3-2 in the Champions League at Old Trafford.
body: Manchester United beat Roma 3-2 at Old Trafford on Tuesday 3 November after trailing 2-0 early on, easing pressure on head coach Michael Carrick. The Irish News, using Press Association copy, said Matias Soule and a Donyell Malen penalty put Roma ahead, with Malen's coming after Ayden Heaven was penalised for handball.

Bruno Fernandes pulled one back in the 58th minute from a retaken penalty, after Roma keeper Devis Vasquez saved the first and Bryan Cristante was ruled to have encroached. Cunha then equalised in the 83rd minute and struck the winner three minutes later. He was sent off for a second booking after an earlier caution for celebrating in the crowd. Fans protested against the Glazer family, and tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch.

The Press Association said United had gone nine matches without a win before the game; it was their third victory of the campaign. Khaleej Times reported that Paris Saint-Germain beat Villarreal 6-0 on the same night to stay perfect and top the table. United host Aston Villa on Sunday.
more.why: The win gives a struggling United and their under-fire coach a reprieve in Europe and a morale boost before a league game.

facts.what: United came from 2-0 down to win 3-2

more.watch: United's next match, at home to Aston Villa on Sunday.

lead.headline: Dozens dead as Russian bombs hit Zaporizhzhia aid point
lead.dek: Ukrainian officials say at least 40 people died and dozens are missing after glide bombs struck a school-turned-shelter in Komyshuvakha.
body: The death toll from a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region rose to 40 on Wednesday, with dozens of people still missing, according to reports from Reuters and the Australian Associated Press. Reuters described it as one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year.

The attack hit the village of Komyshuvakha on Monday 2 November. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russian forces first dropped aerial bombs on an underground school building that was serving as a distribution point as people arrived, then struck the shelter a second time. Classes at the school had been suspended, but it sheltered residents and handed out aid every Monday. Ukraine's national police said the attack included a three-ton FAB bomb fitted with a glide kit; defence intelligence websites say such a weapon carries about 1.4 tons of explosives.

Emergency services said two rescue workers and four police officers were among the dead. Bodycam footage from one of the officers, posted by Ukrainian police and verified by Reuters, shows a warning about incoming glide bombs before a large explosion. Fedorov, co-head of the Zaporizhzhia regional defence council, put the number of missing at 59 on Telegram. Reuters footage from Wednesday showed bodies being loaded into vans while excavators dug beside a large crater and rescuers searched underground. The village lies about 17 km (11 miles) from the nearest Russian positions.

World Central Kitchen, which delivers food and water in the community, described the site as a humanitarian and administrative centre. Its Ukraine response director, Yuliya Stefanyuk, said the strike hit a place where residents were organising help for themselves. Russia's Defence Ministry said it had targeted Ukrainian military units around Komyshuvakha and two other settlements and claimed up to 25 Ukrainian servicemen were killed. Moscow and Kyiv both deny deliberately targeting civilians.

The bombing came a day after a six-day ceasefire expired. That truce, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, allowed nearly 800 people to be evacuated from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, and Zelenskiy awarded her a state honour for the effort. US envoy Steve Witkoff has announced that Washington will host Ukrainian and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November to discuss ending the war, now in its fifth year, along with postwar security and de-escalation. Reuters later reported that the toll climbed further in the days after, as rescuers continued to search the rubble.
lead.why: The strike shows how civilians sheltering and collecting aid remain exposed even as new diplomacy gets under way, and it lands days before the Abu Dhabi talks.

facts.what: Russian aerial bombs hit a school used as a shelter and aid distribution point
facts.when: Monday 2 November; the toll reached 40 by Wednesday
facts.howMuch: At least 40 dead and dozens missing

lead.differ: Early Wednesday figures varied between outlets. Russia's Defence Ministry said it targeted Ukrainian military units; Ukrainian officials said civilians collecting aid were hit.
lead.watch: The rising death toll, and talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November.

more.headline: WHO backs trials of two Bundibugyo Ebola vaccines
more.dek: Tedros announced that the candidates, from Oxford and Moderna, will be added to a trial led by Congo's biomedical institute.
body: The World Health Organization said on Wednesday that it is backing clinical trials of two new vaccines against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, following recommendations from its expert groups. Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus announced the decision at a press conference in Geneva. The candidates are ChAdOx1 BDBV, developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna's mRNA-1469; both were designed specifically for this virus. The trial will be led by the Democratic Republic of Congo's National Institute for Biomedical Research with international partners including the WHO.

The outbreak began in Congo in May and, according to Africa CDC figures cited by Al Jazeera and Africanews, has caused 10,444 confirmed cases and more than 5,300 deaths, with a fatality rate above 50 percent. No vaccine or treatment is designed for the strain. A separate trial that began last month uses Ervebo, which is approved for the Zaire strain of Ebola, not Bundibugyo. Al Jazeera reported that results are expected in early 2027; Africanews gave no start dates or efficacy data.

Tedros stressed that vaccines are not a substitute for proven measures such as early care, contact tracing, isolation and safe burials. He also condemned travel restrictions, which Euronews reported have been imposed on travellers from Congo by Ghana and the United States, saying they penalise countries that share information. Al Jazeera added that a British health worker infected with Ebola is being evacuated to the UK, where the government rates the risk to the public as low.
more.why: With no vaccine tailored to Bundibugyo, the trials are the first formal route to learning whether any shot can slow what is described as the fastest-growing outbreak in Congo's history.

facts.who: The World Health Organization and Congo's National Institute for Biomedical Research
facts.what: Trials of two vaccines made for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola

more.differ: Death figures differ by source: Africa CDC puts deaths at more than 5,300, while Euronews reported a lower count for Congo alone.
more.watch: Al Jazeera reported that trial results are expected in early 2027.

lead.headline: Tankers burn in Hormuz as Iran presses on after US midterms
lead.dek: Iran says mines and fires hit at least five oil tankers and a tugboat on Thursday, even as Qatar and Oman try to keep talks alive.
body: Iran's military said on Thursday 5 November that at least five oil tankers and a tugboat were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz in a string of incidents. The claims came from Iranian state-linked media and officials, and maritime authorities have not independently confirmed them.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps told the Fars news agency that a large tanker trying to use what it called an illegal passageway south of the strait hit a mine, caught fire and stopped. It said a supertanker leaving the eastern end of the strait was halted by a large blaze, and that a tugboat that approached to help also caught fire. The Iranian army later said three more tankers were hit by naval mines and set alight, one east of the strait early in the day and two around noon.

Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that a tanker was struck by two projectiles about 50 nautical miles (93 km) north of Madinat ash-Shamal in Qatar, late on Wednesday. It did not name the ship or its flag, and nobody claimed responsibility. The crew's condition was not known. On 30 October, a Qatari LNG carrier was hit by unidentified objects in the Gulf, though no one was hurt and the ship kept operating.

The strait normally carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil. Iran has restricted traffic there since the US-Israel war on it began on 28 February, and the United States has blockaded Iranian ports. Attacks on shipping are running close to a record pace, and the UK monitoring agency has said it struggles to count them because most vessels no longer report incidents.

Markets reacted cautiously. Brent crude had fallen more than 8 percent on Wednesday to about 94 dollars a barrel, its first close below 100 dollars since September, after the US midterm elections. On Thursday it rose 2.2 percent to about 96.70 dollars, according to CBS News.

The political backdrop is tense. President Donald Trump acknowledged the war had partly hurt Republicans at the polls but said he would do it again, and told the Financial Times he had no immediate plans to strike while the US remained locked and loaded. The New York Times, citing unnamed Pentagon officials, reported that thousands of US personnel on more than a dozen ships and at bases are ready to resume major combat if ordered. Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei dismissed hopes of a change in US policy after the vote and warned that the war would widen if attacks were repeated.

On the diplomatic track, Qatar's Foreign Ministry said both sides were reviewing mediators' proposals, and Oman said it was still working with Iran on a joint mechanism to manage traffic through the strait. Whether those efforts can hold against the mines, the fires and the military buildup is the question for the days ahead.
lead.why: A fifth of the world's oil passes through Hormuz, so each burning tanker raises the risk of a wider war and higher energy prices just as mediators try to keep talks alive.

facts.who: Iran's Revolutionary Guards and army, the United States, mediators in Qatar and Oman
facts.what: Iran said at least five tankers and a tugboat were damaged by mines and fires

lead.differ: The tanker damage claims came from Iranian sources and were not confirmed by maritime authorities; the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency separately reported one tanker hit by projectiles.
lead.watch: Whether the mediators' proposals reviewed by both sides lead to talks, and whether US forces resume major strikes.
lead.india: India buys much of its oil from the Gulf, so trouble in Hormuz can push up fuel prices and shipping costs for Indian buyers.

more.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%, first rise since 2023
more.dek: An 8-1 vote lifted Bank Rate by a quarter point as energy costs push UK inflation higher.
body: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4% on Thursday, up from 3.75%. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1: Governor Andrew Bailey and seven colleagues backed the quarter-point move, while Catherine Mann wanted a half-point rise to 4.25%. It is the bank's first increase in more than three years.

The bank blamed a rise in global energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East. UK inflation reached 3.5% in September, and bank staff expect it to climb to around 4.5% in the first quarter of 2027 and about 5% in the second before energy effects fade. Most members saw the main risk as high energy costs feeding into wages and prices, though evidence of that so far is limited.

Bailey said he could see a case for a further rise if inflation risks do not ease, followed by a more conditional approach. The committee said policy is "not on a pre-set path". Trade press reported that fixed mortgage rates, which follow swap markets, had largely priced in the move, while tracker borrowers would feel it quickly. The next decision is due on 17 December.
more.why: Higher borrowing costs affect mortgage holders and businesses, and the bank is signalling more increases are possible if energy-driven inflation spreads.

facts.who: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee
facts.what: Raised its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4%

more.watch: The next rate decision on 17 December.

more.headline: Astronauts finish ISS solar upgrade in nearly seven-hour spacewalk
more.dek: Anil Menon and Canada's Joshua Kutryk installed the last new roll-out array, completing a project begun in 2021.
body: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk spent just under seven hours outside the International Space Station on Thursday, installing the final roll-out solar array in a power upgrade that began in 2021. CP24 reported the walk began shortly after 8:30 a.m. Eastern and lasted 6 hours 59 minutes; the Canadarm2 robotic arm helped move the array into place.

NASA says the upgrade lifts the station's power generation from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts, while the Canadian report cited an increase of up to 30 per cent. It was the ninth spacewalk of 2026 and the 280th overall. Kutryk, who launched on 1 October with the Crew-13 mission, was making his second walk after 29 October, and it was Menon's fifth.

Seven people are aboard the station. Besides the two spacewalkers, NASA's Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney helped from inside, along with Russian cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov, according to Fox 13.
more.why: The finished upgrade gives the ageing station more electrical capacity for research and operations over the rest of its life.

facts.who: Astronauts Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk
facts.what: Installed the last roll-out solar array on the International Space Station

lead.headline: Paraguay's Senate removes president over bank collapse; Alliana sworn in
lead.dek: Santiago Peña was ousted and placed under house arrest days after the Ueno Bank failure locked millions out of their savings.
body: Paraguay's Senate voted on Friday to remove President Santiago Peña from office, and Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in the same day to serve out the term, which ends in August 2028. Al Jazeera reported that 44 of the Senate's 45 members voted for removal, with one abstention; the Associated Press reported that all 44 senators present voted in favour. Peña is the second Paraguayan president removed by impeachment since the end of Alfredo Stroessner's dictatorship in 1989, according to AP.

Shortly after the vote, prosecutors ordered Peña confined to one of his homes in Asunción on suspicion of breach of trust, influence peddling and using public office for personal gain, AP said. He was told to appear before prosecutors on Saturday morning. The offences carry up to ten years in prison, and he denies wrongdoing. An arrest warrant was also issued for Carlos Carvallo, who headed the finance company that became Ueno before Peña made him central bank chief in 2023. At least 27 people face criminal charges in the scandal, Al Jazeera reported.

The crisis began on Tuesday, when the central bank seized Ueno after it fell below solvency requirements. The bank had around three million customers, close to two-thirds of Paraguay's adults, and held roughly $800 million in public money, including about $355 million of state pension funds, according to Al Jazeera. Customers lost access to accounts and pension payments. Peña had been identified as a shareholder in Ueno's parent company in 2023 and says he sold his stake in early 2025.

The sequence moved quickly. On Thursday Peña offered his resignation, but Congress declined it and the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him. Opposition lawmakers argued that accepting a resignation would have let him keep a seat as a senator for life, with protections against prosecution. In a social media post after his removal, Peña said he was leaving with gratitude and acknowledged the anguish of people still waiting for answers. He did not attend the hearings and sent lawyers instead.

Former president Horacio Cartes, the Colorado Party leader, said the party backed impeachment to restore the country's institutions. Alliana, 52, was vice president under Peña and a former governor of Ñeembucú department who also led the Chamber of Deputies. The lower house declined to open impeachment proceedings against him, though AP reported he is also under investigation in connection with the bank. On taking office he said the country has urgent needs.

Attention now turns to returning depositors' money and to the criminal cases. Congress passed a law this week requiring a state guarantee fund to repay stranded customers within five business days, with payouts that began Thursday, according to AP's earlier reporting, and prosecutors say their investigations will continue.
lead.why: A president once welcomed in Washington as a regional ally has been removed within days by a bank failure that hit most of the adult population, testing Paraguay's institutions and its recently improved credit standing.

facts.who: Paraguay's Senate, Santiago Peña and Pedro Alliana
facts.what: Peña was removed from office and Alliana sworn in
facts.why: The collapse of Ueno Bank, which locked millions of customers out of their savings

lead.differ: Al Jazeera reported 44 of 45 senators voted for removal with one abstention; AP said all 44 senators present voted in favour.
lead.watch: Peña's questioning by prosecutors, the criminal cases, and repayment of stranded depositors.

more.headline: October 2026 was the warmest October on record, EU monitor says
more.dek: Copernicus says 2026 is all but certain to pass 1.5C above pre-industrial levels as a strong El Niño builds.
body: The EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service said on Friday that October 2026 was the warmest October ever recorded, with an average global surface air temperature of 15.35C, according to Down To Earth. That was 1.75C above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average and 0.9C above the 1991-2020 average. Reuters reported that it was the third month in a row above 1.5C, after August and September.

Copernicus puts the 2026 annual average between 1.56C and 1.61C above pre-industrial levels and gives about an 80% chance that the year ranks second-warmest, behind 2024, and a 20% chance it ties or beats it. It would be only the second calendar year above 1.5C. The 2023-2026 four-year average is also expected to exceed that mark. The Paris Agreement target refers to a long-term average, so a single year above 1.5C does not by itself breach it.

Oceans were also at records. Sea surface temperature outside the polar regions averaged 20.95C, the highest for any October, and the Niño 3.4 region of the tropical Pacific reached an anomaly of 3.21C, higher than the peaks of earlier strong El Niño events, with the event still intensifying. Samantha Burgess of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts said El Niño is adding heat to a climate already warmed by human activity.
more.why: The figures arrive days before the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, and show how far the world is running above the Paris Agreement's 1.5C goal.

facts.who: The EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service
facts.what: October 2026 was the warmest October on record

more.watch: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, and whether 2026 ends as the warmest year on record.
more.india: A strong El Niño has in past years been linked to weaker monsoon rains in India, so forecasters will watch next year's monsoon closely.

more.headline: Russell Brand convicted of rape and three sexual assaults in London
more.dek: The comedian was remanded in custody after a jury at Southwark Crown Court returned mixed verdicts; sentencing is set for Monday.
body: Russell Brand, 51, was found guilty at Southwark Crown Court of one count of rape and three of sexual assault, and was acquitted of two other rape counts and one attempted indecent assault, according to AP and Australian Associated Press coverage. The jury of eight men and four women deliberated for more than eight hours. The verdicts came on Thursday and dominated coverage on Friday. The convictions relate to incidents between 2004 and 2009, including an alleged rape of a fan at his home in 2009.

Judge Joel Bennathan refused bail, citing the risk that Brand would flee, and said a prison term of some length would follow. Brand denied the charges and told the court he never forced anyone. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones had called him a ruthless sexual predator, while the defence argued the complainants' accounts were shaped by a 2023 documentary featuring allegations against him. Police have passed prosecutors files on two further rape allegations, AP reported.

Brand rose to fame in the early 2000s through stand-up, television and radio, appeared in Hollywood films and was briefly married to singer Katy Perry. He later built an online following with wellness and religious content.
more.why: The verdict closes a case that began with a 2023 media investigation and marks a major reckoning for one of Britain's best-known entertainers.

facts.what: Convicted of one rape and three sexual assaults; cleared of three other charges

lead.headline: Gunman kills six in Kraków's Main Square; Poland calls it terrorism
lead.dek: A 24-year-old Polish man opened fire from a car in the city's historic centre, and police later found three relatives dead at his home.
body: A gunman killed six people and wounded around 15 more on Saturday afternoon in Kraków's Main Market Square, one of Poland's busiest tourist destinations. A tram driver raised the alarm at about 3 p.m., reporting that a man in a moving car had fired at his tram near the square and shattered the cab window, according to Associated Press reporting carried by PBS.

Police said the attacker, a Polish citizen, drove into the square in military-style fatigues and fired a military-type long gun at random people. Euronews reported he was masked and armed with a semi-automatic rifle resembling an AR-15, plus a pistol, and that more weapons and ammunition were found in his car. He was shot and wounded in a gunfight with officers a short distance away, then detained and taken to hospital. Police said he acted alone. Euronews counted six dead and 16 injured, including two police officers and the suspect himself; the AP's regional toll was six dead and 15 wounded, and early reports had put the dead at five.

Euronews said the suspect is 24 and from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, with no prior convictions and a firearms licence. It reported that Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said he held "very radical views" and was drawn to far-right ideologies, and that Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz denied reports he had served in the armed forces. Police also found the bodies of his father, mother and sister at the family home; they reportedly had gunshot wounds. The victims in the square included four women and two men, one of them a British citizen, with Portuguese and Russian nationals among the injured.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the attack as terrorism and named two senior constables, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, as the officers who detained the suspect; one officer was reported in serious condition. President Karol Nawrocki said his thoughts were with victims and families, and US Ambassador Tom Rose called it a "savage and murderous attack" on Poland's peace.

Mass shootings are rare in Poland, and Kraków draws around 15 million visitors a year, most passing through the Main Square. Poland declared two days of national mourning from midnight on Sunday, with flags at half-mast and entertainment events cancelled. Investigators have yet to set out a full motive, and the suspect's condition and the exact circumstances of his family's deaths remain subjects of the inquiry.
lead.why: A rare act of mass violence in a major European tourist city, officially treated as terrorism and linked by ministers to far-right ideology, is likely to shape Poland's debate on extremism and firearms licensing.

facts.what: A shooting in the city's Main Market Square

lead.differ: AP counted six dead and 15 wounded; Euronews counted 16 injured, including the suspect and two police officers.
lead.watch: The suspect's questioning once doctors allow it, formal charges, and Poland's two days of national mourning.

more.headline: All Blacks beat Scotland 43-21 despite Ashman's historic hat-trick
more.dek: New Zealand scored seven tries at Murrayfield to stay unbeaten against Scotland in the Nations Championship.
body: New Zealand beat Scotland 43-21 at Murrayfield on Saturday in the Nations Championship, collecting a bonus point and extending their long unbeaten record against the Scots. Scotland hooker Ewan Ashman scored a first-half hat-trick, the first by a Scot against the All Blacks according to Yahoo Sports' match report, and Finn Russell converted all three.

The game was close early. The All Blacks led 17-7 after tries from Wallace Sititi, Ethan de Groot and Codie Taylor, but Ashman's second and third tries, the latter from a driving maul, cut the gap to 24-21 at the break after Beauden Barrett had scored. Scotland did not score again. After captain Sione Tuipulotu was sent to the sin-bin for repeated infringements, Barrett crossed for a second time, followed by Josh Moorby and replacement hooker Asafo Aumua, who sealed the win with 13 minutes left.

Barrett's double took him to 50 Test tries, making him the second All Black to reach that mark after Will Jordan. New Zealand have won 32 of their 34 Tests against Scotland, drawing two, and the AP report said the result left them level with South Africa on 20 points in the southern hemisphere standings. South Africa beat Italy 66-7 in Turin the same day. Sources differ slightly on which All Blacks players scored the first-half tries.
more.why: The result keeps New Zealand in the hunt for the inaugural Nations Championship final while extending Scotland's wait for a first win over them.

facts.what: New Zealand won 43-21 with seven tries

more.differ: Match reports differ on which New Zealand players scored the first-half tries.

lead.headline: US opens land and Caspian front against Iran with Task Force Iron Gate
lead.dek: CENTCOM extends its months-long naval blockade to Iran's borders as strikes, mine claims and Qatari-mediated talks continue side by side.
body: US Central Command announced a new unit on Saturday, 7 November, aimed at cutting off the routes Iran uses to bring weapons and other materials in by land. Called Task Force Iron Gate, it widens the naval blockade of Iranian ports that Washington has enforced for months to cover Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.

The unit is small. Reports put it at about 20 civilian and military personnel, based in Tampa, Florida, working with other US agencies to stop advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and what the command calls illegal revenue streams. CENTCOM chief Admiral Brad Cooper said it reinforces the success of the blockade at sea. CBS News noted that the announcement did not explain how the task force would operate, whether it would involve military action, or whether US ships could even work on the Caspian.

The command says the sea blockade has kept more than $25 billion of Iranian crude off the market. It also says that since July US forces have turned back 147 commercial vessels and disabled five that refused to comply. On Saturday an aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of the St Kitts-flagged cargo ship M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman after its crew was told to leave the targeted areas.

Analysts were split on how much it matters. Michael Mulroy, a former Pentagon Middle East official, called it mainly a coordination body, but said any escalation ordered by President Donald Trump would probably hit economic and infrastructure targets rather than the military sites struck earlier in the war. Qatar University's Mahjoob Zweiri said the effort may be largely symbolic, since the US has no Caspian presence and Azerbaijan or Armenia would be unlikely to help for fear of upsetting Russia. Rami Khouri of the American University of Beirut argued that Iran's old trading networks make sealing every route close to impossible. Al Jazeera lists seven land neighbours: Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey and Turkmenistan.

Tehran dismissed the move. A Revolutionary Guards spokesman, quoted by Fars, called it a play on words and said Washington cannot collapse Iran's economy this way. Iran's state news agency reported explosions on Qeshm Island and in Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas. Trump had confirmed minor strikes on Qeshm the day before, saying a small anti-aircraft device was knocked out within minutes. The Guards also said two more tankers hit sea mines near Hormuz, though CBS reported that no maritime officials had confirmed Iran's mine claims and that Trump accuses Tehran of inventing them.

Diplomacy has not stopped. Trump spoke with Qatar's emir on Thursday about ending the war, and Qatari-mediated talks continue. Al Jazeera, citing the Wall Street Journal, reports that Cooper and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are among those urging Trump to resume attacks, while former Trump aide Joe Kent argues the task force undermines the vice president's diplomatic track.
lead.why: The new unit signals that Washington is widening economic pressure on Iran just as talks and strikes run in parallel, and it could draw in Russia and Iran's neighbours.

facts.who: US Central Command, Iran's Revolutionary Guards
facts.what: A new unit, Task Force Iron Gate, to cut Iran's land and Caspian supply routes
facts.howMuch: About 20 staff, based in Tampa, Florida

lead.differ: Analysts disagreed: one former Pentagon official called it mainly a coordination body, while others said it may be largely symbolic because the US has no presence on the Caspian.
lead.watch: Whether Qatari-mediated talks continue, and whether Trump orders new attacks.

more.headline: UN-backed reports warn overshooting 1.5C would damage Earth's ice irreversibly
more.dek: Scientists say even a temporary breach of the Paris limit could affect glaciers, sea ice and permafrost for centuries.
body: Two reports released at the start of November warn that exceeding 1.5C of global warming, even temporarily, would cause large-scale and in many cases irreversible damage to the world's frozen regions. One, titled Overshoot and the Cryosphere, was written with more than 80 scientists by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative with the UN Environment Programme. Its lead author is glaciologist James Kirkham.

AFP reported that warming has reached 1.37C above pre-industrial levels and that Copernicus projects 1.5C could be passed around 2030. The authors say current warming is already unsafe for the Arctic, Antarctic and mountain glaciers, and that a safe level for ice may be near 1C or lower. They cite Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets melting about six times faster than in the 1990s. Above 2.8C, sea level rise could reach up to 5cm a year by 2150, against 0.45cm a year now, and permafrost thaw could release each year about as much carbon dioxide as the United States emits.

Some glaciers and sea ice could partly recover if temperatures fall back, but Matthew England of the University of New South Wales said that could take decades to centuries. The reports urge keeping any overshoot as small and brief as possible and cutting fossil fuel use faster. Kirkham argued that a temporary breach makes the Paris goals more urgent, not irrelevant.
more.why: The reports argue that even a short breach of the 1.5C limit would have lasting costs for ice, water supplies and sea levels.

facts.who: The International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the UN Environment Programme
facts.what: Reports warning that overshooting 1.5C would do lasting damage to Earth's ice
facts.when: Released at the start of November

more.india: Himalayan glaciers feed rivers that millions of Indians rely on, so lasting damage to mountain ice could matter for water supplies.
